item.title: China brings legacy of Tokyo Trial to UN Headquarters with exhibition marking 80th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 07:51:00
People view exhibits at an exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial at the UN Headquarters in New York, Oct. 26, 2026. An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday. Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo) An exhibition marking the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trial opened at UN Headquarters in New York on Monday. Titled "Justice and Peace for All Humanity," the exhibition features historical photographs, archival documents and publications on the investigation and prosecution of Japanese war crimes during World War II. "The Tokyo Trial cements the post-war world order, upholds fairness and justice, and advances international rule of law. It is a landmark victory of peace over war, civilization over barbarism, and justice over evil, with far-reaching political and historical significance," said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations, at the opening ceremony. "The Tokyo Trial put Japanese militarism in the dock. It's essential for Japan to bear in mind what is at the core of the trial, make a clean break with militarism, and commit itself to peace once and for all," he said. "Regrettably, right-wing forces in Japan keep questioning the legitimacy of the Tokyo Trial under various pretexts, and try to gloss over Japan's history of aggression. From worshiping Class-A war criminals to hollowing out the pacifist Constitution, from easing controls on arms exports to lifting the ban on the right to collective self-defense, Japan is going further away from the Tokyo Trial and tearing up its 'pacifist' rulebook." "History, if not forgotten, can serve as a guide for the future," said Fu. "We need to guard against rising neo-militarism, and together uphold the post-war order and international peace and security." Qi Dahai, director-general of the Department of Treaty and Law of China's Foreign Ministry, Zhou Feng, curator of the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, and officials from Russia and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea addressed the opening ceremony. Permanent representatives to the United Nations from Spain, Nicaragua and other countries attended the ceremony. Speakers highlighted the Tokyo Trial's role in upholding peace through the rule of law and bringing Japan's wartime aggression to justice. They stressed the need to learn from history, remember the suffering caused by war, and work together to prevent the resurgence of militarism and aggression. Organized by China's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, the exhibition is being held during the UN International Law Week. item.title: China sends defense attaché to ADMM-Plus; Philippines to blame for participation downgrade: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 07:45:00
A person walks past a logo of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) at a hotel serving as the international media center for the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) and the 13th ADMM-Plus in Cebu City, Philippines, October 27, 2026. Photo: VCG The Chinese Defense Ministry announced that China will send the defense attaché of the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines to attend the 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Cebu, which marks the lowest-level Chinese representation at the ADMM-Plus since its inaugural session in 2010. Analysts told the Global Times that the downgraded attendance is attributable to the Philippines. The defense attaché of the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines will represent the Chinese side to attend the 13th ADMM-Plus in Cebu on October 29. During the event, the Chinese side will exchange views with other parties on upholding dialogue and enhancing mutual understanding and trust, and reiterate China's firm support to ASEAN centrality in the regional architecture to promote regional defense and security dialogue and cooperation, and safeguard peace and stability in the region, Chinese Ministry of National Defense said in a statement on Tuesday. According to ASEAN’s official website, the 20th ADMM, the 13th ADMM Plus and associated side meetings will be held in Cebu, the Philippines, on October 28-29. The Philippines holds the ASEAN chairmanship for 2026. The inaugural ADMM-Plus was held in 2010. As a key component of the regional security architecture, the ADMM-Plus facilitates cooperation between the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and its eight dialogue partners to address shared security challenges. The Global Times has learned from sources that this marks the lowest rank of Chinese representation since 2010. Except for the 10th ADMM-Plus in 2023, which was attended by a delegation from China’s Ministry of National Defense, the other 11 sessions were all attended by the then Chinese minister of national defense. China’s downgraded attendance at the ADMM-Plus reflects the current state of China-Philippines political, diplomatic and defense ties. The Philippines bears responsibility for this situation, Ding Duo, director of the Research Center for International and Regional Issues at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times. Ding said that as the ASEAN chair and host this year, the Philippines should have earnestly fulfilled its chairmanship duties, properly organized the meeting, managed the agenda, and fostered a calm, constructive and cooperation-focused atmosphere for dialogue and consultation among all parties. Instead, it has done the opposite: turning the multilateral platform into an arena to hype up the South China Sea issue and advance its own narrow interests. Worse still, it should not allow its military and law-enforcement agencies to hijack the agenda, smear China and stoke confrontation, said the expert. The Chinese Embassy in Manila also said in a post on X on October 19 that “Recently, Philippine military and law enforcement personnel, along with anti-China forces, have been actively undermining China-Philippines relations, engaging in extensive rights violations and provocations at sea in an attempt to create incidents. The number of such incidents has doubled compared with the past.” “In particular, the Philippines' Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., a representative of anti-China forces within the country’s military and law-enforcement establishment, has repeatedly launched attacks, smears and groundless accusations against China regarding China-related and maritime issues recently, severely undermining the atmosphere necessary for the development of bilateral ties,” Ding said. The expert noted that Philippine President Marcos Jr. has failed to effectively rein in domestic anti-China forces and has even adopted a laissez-faire stance, taking no action against individuals or remarks that harm China-Philippines ties. “Furthermore, with external countries, including the US and Japan, continuing to meddle in the South China Sea issue and ramping up support for the Philippines, there are no favorable conditions for bilateral relations to improve,” said Ding. It can be anticipated that as this year’s ASEAN chair, the Philippine military and law-enforcement agencies will seek to hijack dialogue agendas on occasions including China-ASEAN summits, hype up the so-called “South China Sea threat” and smear China’s South China Sea policy through formal meetings or sideline events, said Ding. “Under such circumstances, by sending a representative to the meeting, China aims to clarify its position and propositions and to firmly respond to the Philippines’ attacks and smears. On the other hand, China will not endorse such activities, much less lend any form of support to them,” Ding said. During a press conference on Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that “The ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting Plus is meant to play a positive role in enabling regional countries to step up dialogue, increase trust and promote cooperation. We oppose attempts by anyone to use this platform to seek selfish gains, hijack ASEAN and create trouble.”

item.title: Philippine warship 'trailing' Chinese aircraft carrier Liaoning? The whole world is laughing: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 00:31:00
The Liaoning aircraft carrier participates in a dual-aircraft-carrier formation drill on October 21, 2024. Photo: VCG The Philippine side is well aware of the consequences of recklessly provoking China, yet it has still pressed ahead with this self-staged farce. The root cause is that certain forces in the Philippines want to stir up trouble in the South China Sea to contain China, but lack the confidence and capabilities to back up any substantive confrontational moves. All they can do is resort to this shoddy performance to bluff and create a false impression of strength. Recently, during a new round of multilateral maritime cooperative activity involving the US, Japan and the Philippines, Manila dispatched a vessel to follow the Liaoning aircraft carrier group. At most, the Philippine vessel trailed the Chinese carrier group from a distance and snapped a few photos. Yet the Philippine side hyped this up as an operation to "track" and "monitor" the Chinese navy. Judging solely by the rhetoric of some Philippine military figures and media outlets, one might assume that Manila had deployed a formidable naval force. But once all the relevant facts are considered, the true nature of this guilty-minded performance becomes clear. The aircraft carrier Liaoning 's training activities in the relevant waters of the Western Pacific are routine arrangements under its annual training plan, consistent with international law and international practice, and not directed against any particular country or target. As the group navigated through the high seas and archipelagic sea lanes, it exercised the rights of navigation and passage guaranteed under international law. Throughout the voyage, the group maintained a professional and restrained posture and did not take any hostile action against the Philippines. Even a Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson had to acknowledge that "the movement could still fall within internationally recognized navigational rights." The BRP Sarangani, the Philippine vessel involved in the operation, was originally a decommissioned patrol and rescue vessel donated by the Taiwan authorities. Given its size, its so-called "tracking" of a large combat formation such as an aircraft carrier group could amount to little more than symbolic shadowing from a distance. It could neither approach the aircraft carrier group nor gather much valuable intelligence, let alone establish any meaningful monitoring capability. The Philippine side is well aware of the consequences of recklessly provoking China, yet it has still pressed ahead with this self-staged farce. The root cause is that certain forces in the Philippines want to stir up trouble in the South China Sea to contain China, but lack the confidence and capabilities to back up any substantive confrontational moves. All they can do is resort to this shoddy performance to bluff and create a false impression of strength. Looking deeper, this maneuver is driven both by domestic political calculations in the Philippines and by a desire to appease external powers. Faced with challenges such as sluggish economic growth and mounting pressure on the government, Manila is attempting to divert public attention by hyping up external "threats" and projecting an image of being "tough on the outside," thereby reaping political capital for the administration. Meanwhile, the Philippines has been stepping up military cooperation with the US, Japan and other countries. Publicizing details of its so-called "monitoring" of the Liaoning aircraft carrier group amid joint US-Japan-Philippines exercises serves to demonstrate its value to external allies in maintaining a "forward presence" and to show that it can make tangible contributions, even if that "contribution" amounts to nothing more than a decommissioned small vessel trailing the carrier group from a distance. It is also an attempt to enlist external support to bolster its position in maritime disputes and exploit regional tensions for unwarranted gains. But no matter how inflated the bubble of rhetoric becomes, it cannot deliver real security. Some in the Philippines also need to carefully consider the costs of their blind faith in courting powers from outside the region. Certain external powers are willing to put the Philippines on the front line because doing so serves their own strategic interests. This does not mean, however, that they are prepared to bear the consequences of every risky move Manila makes. Should an incident occur at sea, Philippine vessels and personnel would be closest to the scene, and the Philippines itself would be the first to bear the risks. Pinning the country's maritime security on the appearance of backing from others not only overestimates the practical value of that retired patrol boat but also underestimates the price the Philippines itself would have to pay if regional tensions escalated. In fact, what truly threatens regional security is the Philippines' provocations in the South China Sea and its collusion with the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in Taiwan island. The Taiwan question is particularly sensitive. Any move that could blur the boundaries of the one-China policy or extend security cooperation into sensitive areas risks triggering major upheaval in the region. On the one hand, Manila reiterates its adherence to the one-China policy; on the other, it allows coast guard equipment from the Taiwan region to enter the ranks of its coast guard. Such double-dealing is playing with fire. China remains unwavering in its commitment to safeguarding national sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, while consistently advocating negotiations to manage differences. The Liaoning aircraft carrier's voyages into distant waters are a normal milestone in China's defense modernization. Its course will not be altered by the trailing of one or two decommissioned patrol vessels, nor will it be diverted by the clamor surrounding a handful of joint military exercises. Manila must understand that stirring up trouble with the backing of external powers will not bring it genuine security. It will only draw the Philippines deeper into a complex geopolitical game.

item.title: Chinese defense firm introduces 40mm cased telescoped ammunition, already fielded by multiple domestic platforms
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 22:41:00
Type 100 support vehicles are reviewed at China's V-Day military parade on September 3, 2025. Photo: Screenshot from Changan Wangjiang A new Chinese 40mm cased telescoped ammunition round can punch through 130 millimeters of homogeneous steel armor from a kilometer away - firepower that leaves conventional shells far behind - while offering three damage modes: armor-piercing, high-explosive fragmentation and programmable airburst. The round is already being used by multiple domestic weapons platforms, a Chinese state-owned defense company said on Monday, while providing footage showing the Type 100 support vehicles and new-generation airborne combat vehicles that debuted during the 2025 V-Day military parade. The projectile of the telescoped ammunition is enclosed inside the cartridge case, making the entire round a single cylinder. A single shot can punch through 130 millimeters of homogeneous steel armor, and easily deal with field fortifications and low, slow and small (LSS) aerial targets, said Changan Wangjiang, a defense company under the China South Industries Group, in a video released on its official social media account on WeChat on Monday. An ammunition storage box inside a vehicle armed with domestic 40mm cased telescoped rounds Photo: Screenshot from Changan Wangjiang The round uses a disruptive two-stage ignition design: the first ignition separates the projectile structure and drives the projectile into a locked position, letting the cartridge case form a sealed chamber. A second ignition then sends the round flying at meteoric speed, giving the cased telescoped ammunition its formidable striking power. The round also uses a dart-like aerodynamic layout and fin stabilization, achieving accuracy of 0.5 meters by 0.5 meters at one kilometer, making it not only powerful, but precise enough for near-perfect hits. The 40mm round currently has three main damage modes. The round's first damage mode is the armor penetration mode. Able to punch through 130mm of steel plate from a kilometer away, it can seriously damage main battle tanks. Its second mode, high-explosive fragmentation, sends blast waves in all directions upon impact. Just a few rounds can destroy fortifications and bunkers. The third, programmable airburst, detonates the shell midair to form a dense barrage that leaves drones and other low-slow-small aerial targets nowhere to hide. Cased telescoped ammunition is not new, the concept has existed for years. China pursued it for several reasons, Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times. First, tanks and armored vehicles have limited internal space, so cased telescoped rounds allow more ammunition to be carried. Second, they hold more propellant, giving greater striking power. They also generate relatively low recoil and have a neat, regular shape that makes transport easier. The 40mm round is already being used with multiple domestically produced weapons, achieving seamless coverage across all terrains and time periods, a development set to begin a new era of smarter, more efficient Chinese equipment, according to Changan Wangjiang. The information about the new round accompanied footage of Type 100 support vehicles and new-generation domestic airborne combat vehicles, both of which debuted at the V-Day military parade held in Beijing on September 3, 2025. The Type 100 support vehicle can collaborate with the Type 100 tank. While the tank's main gun has strong firepower, the tank faces challenges in engaging multiple targets simultaneously. This is when the fire support vehicle comes in, using its higher rate of fire to suppress and eliminate unarmored targets such as foot soldiers operating anti-tank missiles or lightly armored vehicles, an expert told the Global Times in a previous interview. Airborne combat vehicles can be transported across long distances via the air and provide heavily armored mobile support. They act as the airborne edges in the PLA's fast response and deep strike operations. The large-scale fielding of specially improved conventional munitions shows that the PLA's overall ammunition design philosophy is becoming more forward-looking and more efficient, Song added.

item.title: GT Voice: China's AI stock pullback isn't a signal of a 'bubble bursting'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 22:14:00
AI Photo: VCG The recent lackluster performance of China's STAR 50 Index, which tracks the 50 largest stocks on the sci-tech innovation board, has drawn attention, with some Western media outlets seizing on the pullback to draw misleading conclusions about the country's artificial intelligence (AI) development. Reuters on Monday published an article headlined "In China, the AI bubble has already burst," interpreting the drop in the AI-heavy STAR 50 Index and the contraction in the market capitalization of AI-related listed companies as the bursting of bubbles. Short-term stock price fluctuations reflect shifts in capital preferences, market expectations and valuations, and they do not necessarily signal a reversal in an industry's fundamentals. To equate an index decline with a "bursting bubble," and to treat capital market movements as a denial of China's AI industry prospects, is logically untenable and gives a misleading picture of China's technological development. Capital markets naturally experience cycles of rising and falling expectations and valuation corrections, and volatility in sci-tech innovation sectors is particularly fierce. This is a common phenomenon in global financial markets. The sharp pullback in AI and semiconductor-related stocks this round is essentially a correction of the overheated valuations of some targets in the earlier period, and a rational cooling of capital from excessive expectations, rather than a shake-up of the industrial foundation. Figures are more than enough to break the one-sided narrative of the "bubble theory." According to Minister of Industry and Information Technology Li Lecheng, China's core AI industry was valued at more than 1.2 trillion yuan ($173.9 billion) in 2025, as the technology is emerging as a powerful driver for high-quality economic development. AI is increasingly being deployed across factories and daily life in China. As of the end of 2025, more than 30 percent of manufacturing enterprises with annual main business turnover of at least 20 million yuan had adopted AI technologies, while Chinese companies had released more than 300 humanoid robot products. Data released at a State Council Information Office press conference shows that as of the end of June 2026, China's intelligent computing capacity reached 2,185 EFLOPS (Exa Floating-point Operations Per Second), a year-on-year surge of 177 percent, and the overall utilization rate of computing facilities nationwide stood at 71.4 percent. Even more symbolic is that Chinese AI large-language models recorded usage of 93.54 trillion tokens for the week ending October 25, marking 26 consecutive weeks of global leadership, according to data from OpenRouter. This figure shows that the vitality of China's domestic AI application ecosystem has entered the global first tier. These indicators certainly cannot replace profitability, nor can they guarantee that every enterprise will succeed, but they at least show that China's AI sector has a continuously expanding base, a growing number of market players and large-scale computing power support. Given such extensive industrial activity, it is obviously biased to claim that the entire industry is a "bubble that has burst" based solely on a phase of stock price adjustment. Judging the real prospects of a high-tech industry comes down to technological capability, commercial application and economic returns. Whether technology continues to advance and can operate reliably in complex scenarios, and whether applications are moving toward large-scale adoption and can help improve efficiency in manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, education and other sectors - these are the far more meaningful criteria. This process cannot be achieved overnight, nor will it change direction because of a few stock price swings. When evaluating China's science and technology industries, Western media outlets tend to swing between two extremes. When growth is rapid, it portrays China as an "unstoppable threat" and when the market adjusts, it rushes to declare "the bursting of bubbles." These two seemingly opposite narratives actually share the same problem: they are unwilling to understand China's development with a long-term and professional vision. China's AI sector should neither be overestimated nor underestimated. What it needs is continuous innovation, effective competition, and patient capital, rather than being led by short-term noise. In the end, the long-term value of China's AI development will stand the test of time through sustained technological progress, widespread commercial adoption and solid real economic returns. Separating short-term market sentiment from long-term industrial trends is far closer to the facts and carries far more analytical value than simply slapping on a "burst bubble" label.

item.title: GT Economic Investigates: What opportunities does China's AI wave present for Indian software companies?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 21:21:00
Humanoid robots undergo testing and debugging at Shenzhen's first humanoid robot pilot production line in South China's Guangdong Province on April 12, 2026. Photo: VCG Mathivanan Venkatachalam, Global Vice President of ManageEngine, is on a trip to China. He has visited Beijing and is scheduled to meet with a customer in Shenzhen on Wednesday. During this visit, he is tracking developments in China's AI landscape and the digital needs of local enterprises, while gaining a deeper understanding of the Chinese market's operating environment and client requirements. Indian-based ManageEngine, a division of Zoho Corporation and a provider of enterprise IT management solutions, recently rolled out Zia AI agents across its full-stack IT management product suite for the Chinese market. This marks the latest step in the company's efforts to deepen its localization and expand its presence in China. The firm launched more than 30 AI agents in the first batch and plans to increase the number to over 100 by the end of 2026. The upgrade is designed to enhance its full-stack IT management capabilities, automate routine operational tasks and enable autonomous business execution, according to information the company shared with the Global Times. Against the backdrop of fierce global competition in enterprise AI, Indian tech players are stepping up localization efforts in China to cater to the specific needs of local corporate users. Meanwhile, a growing number of Indian firms, driven by cost considerations, are adopting Chinese open-source models such as DeepSeek and Kimi and developing tailored applications based on them. Indian firms have strengths in their abundant tech talent and competitive drive. China, as the world's second-largest economy, boasts solid infrastructure, a complete industrial chain for servers and storage, a massive domestic market and extensive real-world application scenarios - major draws for Indian investors, some Chinese analysts said on Tuesday. China has solid strengths in AI R&D, real-world deployment and foundation model ecosystem development, while India has rich experience and talent in global IT services, software outsourcing and enterprise solution delivery. The two sides have promising prospects for AI cooperation and can deepen collaboration in R&D, market expansion and standard-setting to support the healthy development of the global AI industry, they noted. Expanding footprint During Venkatachalam's visit to Beijing, ManageEngine, which has been in the Chinese market for about 20 years, announced that it will invest 425 million yuan ($63.73 million) in the Chinese market over the next five years, with funds primarily allocated to data center construction, AI R&D, technical support system development, and strengthening its partner ecosystem. To date, ManageEngine has served over 5,000 enterprises in China and has established partnerships with more than 100 organizations. Given that overseas platforms such as Google are not suited for domestic needs, ManageEngine chose to actively engage with China's domestic large-model ecosystem and integrate its products with local large language models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek, Venkatachalam said in an interview with Global Times. Over the past five or six years, ManageEngine has continued to invest in localization R&D, refining technologies and products to meet the needs of Chinese customers and gradually building localized IT service capabilities. This also an important reason for the company's continued investment in the Chinese market, he added. Amid the global AI boom, a growing number of Indian tech firms are leveraging Chinese LLMs to lower costs and broaden the reach of their AI services. The Indian government has a national AI mission and is encouraging private-sector Indian firms to play an active role in the holistic development of the AI Ecosystem in India, cutting across all verticals. Our organization is exploring cooperation with Global AI models for e-commerce development and delivery services, Mansoor Nadeem Lari, CEO of the India-based Silk Route Trade and Industry Development Corp, told the Global Times. In this regard, Lari said his organization had recently been in touch with Accio Work, an agentic AI platform for international units under Alibaba, which he described as a tool for comprehensive e- commerce services. We will be cooperating in the near future with the Chinese e-commerce AI ecosystem, as it has been instrumental in the massive growth of China's $400 billion cross-border e-commerce exports, Lari added. Lari is not alone. Puneet Kumar, CEO at Mirae Asset Venture Investments India, said that several consumer technology startups that he has met since mid-2025 use such Chinese open-weight LLMs - those that rely on publicly accessible parameters - which help drive down costs by an "order of magnitude," Nikkei Asia reported in July. Because these parameters are publicly available, users can download and modify them on their own computers, in contrast to the proprietary offerings by US frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The Chinese open-weight LLMs can be accessed in India through service providers such as Microsoft at a fraction of the price of their American counterparts, thanks to their low cost of development, the report said. India has a large pool of technical talent and distinctive strengths in higher education. Many of its homegrown enterprises are ambitious and have developed competitive advantages in certain sectors. Meanwhile, China has equally notable strengths: As the world's second-largest economy, it has well-developed infrastructure, a comprehensive industrial chain, a huge domestic market and advanced capabilities in translating technologies into real-world applications. These advantages are key reasons why Indian firms value the Chinese market and choose to establish a presence here, Xiang Ligang, president of the Beijing Institute of Intelligent Era Industry, told the Global Times on Tuesday. Complementary strengths The Indian government has ramped up investment in AI in recent years. In March 2024, it launched the IndiaAI Mission, a national industrial initiative that provides AI startups with digital infrastructure including access to critical GPU computing resources, alongside policy and financial support. India's listed AI market could gain an additional $50 billion to $100 billion in market capitalisation over the next two to five years as privately held AI companies move towards initial public offerings (IPOs), ANI reported on October 21, citing a report by Goldman Sachs. India has a huge population base and diversified market demand, providing broad space for the application of AI technologies. With strong government support, major Indian companies such as Adani, Tata, and Reliance Industries have been continuously increasing investment in AI and data center construction in recent years, boosting the development of India's digital economy, according to media reports. For instance, Tata Communications Ltd. announced investments of close to $450 million on Monday to build high-speed network cables connecting India's AI data-centre corridors, Reuters reported. In Xiang's view, populous India enjoys unique advantages for AI development: its large population underpins a substantial pool of usable data, and its linguistic and cultural diversity yields rich datasets for training advanced AI models. According to Forbes India in March of 2025, India is home to around 3 percent of the world's data centers but produces about 20 percent of the world's data. Xiang noted that India's startup ecosystem continues to mature and its sizable digital public infrastructure (DPI) has developed to a considerable scale. With strengths in IT talent, digital public infrastructure and a fast-growing startup ecosystem, India has considerable potential in the global AI race. China and India do have complementary strengths that provide a solid foundation for AI cooperation. China has accumulated extensive expertise in AI R&D, real-world application deployment and development of the foundation-model ecosystem, while India has extensive experience and a deep talent pool in global IT services, software outsourcing and enterprise-level solution delivery, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times on Tuesday. The two countries have broad prospects for AI cooperation and can deepen collaboration in areas including technology research and development, market expansion and standards-setting to jointly promote the sound development of the global AI industry, Qian said. In practice, some mid-sized Indian IT service providers are using AI to reshape their business models, creating new revenue streams by helping clients reduce the costs of software and AI use. Meanwhile, Indian firms including Krutrim and AceCloud have deployed DeepSeek models on on-premises servers to balance cost and compliance. This "Chinese models plus Indian services" framework leverages the technological and cost advantages of Chinese foundation models alongside the localized service and delivery capabilities of Indian IT companies, serving as a typical example of complementary cooperation, Qian added. Observers also draw a clear distinction between India and China's respective trajectories in AI. China leads the frontier-model race for now, DeepSeek, Qwen and Kimi are some of the widely known open-source models that have successfully beaten the frontier models of the West. India's compute build is real but at an earlier stage, Manish Bhandari, the founder of Vallum Capital Advisors, a Mumbai-based investment management firm told the Global Times. India's IndiaAI Mission had empaneled 18,693 GPUs, including 12,896 H100s, as of early 2025, with plans to roughly double that. That's India's real edge, not out-building China on pre-training economics, but deploying whatever gets open-sourced. An open-weight model hands away the hardest part - training - for free; what's left is fine-tuning, compliance-wrapping, and integrating it into a client's actual infrastructure, which is exactly the muscle Indian IT services and Global Capability Centres have built across every prior enterprise wave, Bhandari said. He also said that, China, among others, keeps open-sourcing models, while Indian IT services keep capturing deployment margin on whichever ones clients choose. Realistic cooperation looks like arm's-length absorption of open models, not joint compute or data-sharing ventures.

item.title: Mbappé apologizes for inappropriate remarks in French, Chinese and English after strong backlash in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 20:51:00
French football player Kylian Mbappé has apologized for his extremely inappropriate remarks that have drawn anger and fierce criticism in China. French football player Kylian Mbappé has apologized for his extremely inappropriate remarks that have drawn anger and fierce criticism in China. In a statement issued on Tuesday and published in French, Chinese and English, he said his comment was "ill-judged" and that "I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world." "I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry," he said in the statement. The apology came after a wave of criticism on Chinese social media, where an interview featuring Mbappé circulated widely at the weekend. At least three Chinese companies have terminated their cooperation with him on Tuesday, and media platforms have taken out content related to the footballer. Content related to Mbappé could no longer be found on news apps operated by China's state broadcaster CCTV and several other platforms as of Tuesday.

item.title: Deep beneath Xinjiang's Ili Basin, an 'invisible' mine extracts uranium without conventional open-pit excavation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 20:49:00
Drilling workers operate in front of a drilling rig in Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang. Photo: Fan Lingzhi/Global Times A row of cylindrical, grayish-black rock samples lay on the ground, awaiting "inspection" by a handheld gamma radiation detector. As the beeping grew increasingly frequent, the readings on the detector continued to climb, drawing gasps of surprise from visitors - the uranium content in these samples had reached a level that made extraction economically viable. Technicians at the Ili base of the No 216 Geological Party of China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region watched with amused smiles. These tests were routine for them, but for the Global Times reporter, it was an entirely novel experience. Uranium was formed billions of years ago through neutron star mergers or supernova explosions. Yet it is scattered so sparsely throughout the Earth's crust that finding it, let alone extracting it safely and efficiently, presents a formidable challenge. That was what brought the Global Times reporter to CNNC Xinjiang Mining Co Ltd and the No 216 Geological Party. As the interview vehicle entered the valley grasslands in October, there were no enormous open pits, nor trucks kicking up clouds of dust. Instead, only a few scattered drilling rigs appeared not far from flocks of sheep grazing leisurely. The "magic" of seemingly producing uranium out of "nothing" was gradually beginning to be revealed. A precise game of 'hide-and-seek' About an hour after leaving the city, the Global Times reporter's vehicle turned off the road into a cornfield. There, on an open patch of ground just 20 to 30 meters from the corn, stood a drilling rig roughly six stories tall. The harvest above ground and the resources hidden beneath it existed side by side. On average, every ton of rock in the Earth's crust contains about 2.5 grams of uranium. Although uranium is more abundant than elements such as gold, silver, mercury and tungsten, its deposits are widely dispersed underground. Under natural conditions, uranium rarely accumulates into ore bodies with sufficient concentrations for industrial extraction. Therefore, finding commercially viable uranium deposits has long been a major challenge in geological exploration. That was why the sight of the somewhat "slender" core drilling rig came as a surprise to the reporter. The difficult task of prospecting for valuable uranium deposits turned out to look remarkably unassuming. Three individual drill rods, each measuring 4.6 meters long, were joined together using trapezoidal threaded connections to form a long drill stand. A worker dressed in a blue uniform was operating the machinery, pulling the drill rods out of the ground one by one and skillfully unscrewing their threaded connections. Black drilling mud streamed down the rods as they were removed. The rods were then stood upright on a rack nearby, ready to be lowered back into the ground after the core samples had been retrieved. Drilling at a particular location does not necessarily mean that uranium has been found there. Given the difficulty of drilling operations and the complexity of geological conditions, uranium can sometimes seem to be playing "hide-and-seek" with prospectors. On a geological cross-section of the mining area, the Global Times reporter could see just how difficult the search could be. Uranium deposits appeared like a ribbon drifting through the Earth's crust. It was precisely this seemingly unpredictable distribution that posed such an enormous challenge to exploration: Drill a little too deep or too shallow, and the deposit could easily be missed. To locate uranium deposits as precisely as possible, long periods of fieldwork are a routine part of prospectors' lives. The Global Times reporter lifted the curtain at the entrance to a prefabricated cabin. Inside were six beds. Although the space was small, it was fully equipped with bottled water, toiletries and other necessities. "We have pretty much everything we need here, but when you spend so much time in the field, the hardest part is missing home," one worker told the Global Times. Yet it is through these arduous years of field exploration that some prospectors have achieved remarkable results. One particularly telling story was that of Wang Zhiru, a master drilling technician at CNNC Xinjiang Mining and a model worker of the autonomous region. In 1996, Wang, then a 24-year-old young man from a farming family in Northwest China's Gansu Province, crossed the Tianshan Mountains to join Factory 737 of Tianshan Uranium Industry, known as the "cradle of in-situ leaching." In his diary, he wrote: "Let yellow sand be my paper and the drill rod my pen; I vow to write my youth into the earth." Over the following 29 years, he handled more than 400 downhole drilling accidents and applied for 21 patents. He even set a record of working continuously for 72 hours in the scorching sands of Shihongtan in Turpan, where temperatures exceeded 40 C. Wang Chunli, a former head of the No 316 Brigade, described him as "a technology fanatic who puts his life on the line." His daughter treasures a family photograph taken in front of a drilling derrick on her phone. "Dad's office is up on the drilling rig," she said. Aerial view of Plant 735 of CNNC Xinjiang Mining in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: Courtesy of CNNC Keeping uranium extraction beneath rock layers Finding the right ore body is only the first challenge. How to extract uranium from the rock through leaching is another. Leaving the exploration site, the Global Times reporter arrived at Plant 735 of CNNC Xinjiang Mining, once home to China's first and largest standalone in-situ uranium leaching demonstration project. The answer to this second challenge lies in a technology known as "neutral in-situ uranium leaching." The magnificent Tianshan Mountains in the distance stole the spotlight from the plant itself, becoming the first sight to catch visitors' attention. Then, the scattered blue and red numbered "posts" dotting the grassland come into view. Tang Yiwei, deputy director of Plant 735 of CNNC Xinjiang Mining, told the Global Times that these were the key components of in-situ uranium leaching: process wells. The blue ones were injection wells, while the red ones were extraction wells. These process wells originated from the exploration boreholes mentioned earlier. Once geological exploration has established the underground conditions and confirmed that a deposit is worth developing, a plant can be built to begin "mining" the uranium. A leaching solution is injected into the ore-bearing layer through injection wells to dissolve the uranium-bearing components of the ore. The uranium-rich solution is then pumped out through extraction wells and transferred to a hydrometallurgical plant for further purification. The entire process takes place in a closed underground system, leaving no visible traces of conventional tunnel excavation on the surface. That explains why the plant bears virtually no resemblance to a traditional mining site. Tang explained that uranium mining and metallurgy technologies have gone through three generations of development. Beginning in 1964, the Xinjiang Mining and Metallurgy Bureau adopted conventional uranium extraction methods to recover uranium from uranium-bearing lignite. In 1987, it began experimenting with acid in-situ leaching, achieving breakthroughs in key technologies. Today, Plant 735 uses third-generation neutral in-situ uranium leaching, with carbon dioxide and oxygen serving as the leaching agents. "Some uranium deposits in the Ili basin contain high levels of carbonates, making them suitable for neutral in-situ uranium leaching. By controlling and adjusting the amounts of carbon dioxide and oxygen added, we can prevent chemical precipitation within the system and achieve efficient, environmentally friendly leaching. It is a neutral, mild and green in-situ uranium extraction process," Tang said. In addition, the mining area uses a five-spot well pattern designed according to the direction of groundwater flow, ensuring a clearly structured operating process. The Global Times reporter entered a room covering more than 100 square meters, where instruments resembling water meters were neatly arranged in rows. Tang explained that this was the plant's central control room, which could accurately display the real-time conditions of each injection well and automatically adjust the proportions of leaching agents added based on the data. Throughout the interviews, the Global Times reporter repeatedly shifted between feeling utterly bewildered and experiencing sudden moments of clarity. The engineers would often explain complex technical principles before wrapping up with a simple, accessible analogy. According to engineers at CNNC Xinjiang Mining, pragmatism is a defining characteristic of people working in China's nuclear industry. "If you ask the workers what they have accomplished, many will simply say, 'I haven't really done much.' But if you start talking to them about technology or their work, they might go on for hours without stopping." Exploration workers conduct uranium prospecting operations at an undisclosed location in Xinjiang. Photo: VCG Safety under control, incomes on the rise By October, the grass had turned completely yellow, but this did little to diminish the beauty of the sunlit grasslands beneath a vast sky dotted with wispy clouds. "You still came too late. The grasslands are greener and more beautiful in summer!" Tang said. "No matter how advanced the technology is, this is still a uranium mine. Aren't local residents afraid?" the Global Times reporter asked during the journey. Tang led the reporter to an information board. "The amount of radiation received by a resident living near a nuclear power plant over the course of a year is equivalent to the radiation exposure from smoking one cigarette. Radiation is everywhere in daily life. For example, the radiation dose a person receives from a round-trip flight to Europe is comparable to that from a single chest fluoroscopy examination." "To put it more plainly, we are trained in this field and are still willing to work in it for the long term. That shows nuclear energy really isn't something to be afraid of," Tang said with a smile. The Global Times learned that the process of gaining acceptance for in-situ uranium leaching among local residents had not been entirely smooth. Yikebali Xiamixiding, 23, lives in a nearby town. His income of around 8,000 yuan ($1,120) a month from working at Plant 735 is the main source of livelihood for his family of six. "I remember that construction of Plant 735 began in 2013. At the time, I hoped I would be able to work there, but I was also worried about whether the plant would pollute our drinking water or damage the grasslands," Yikebali, whose main job involves drilling, told the Global Times. "In fact, my father started working at Tianshan Uranium Industry back in 2005, and he is still in good health today. He has never been ill, which also suggests that the plant has not caused pollution. Although drilling is carried out here, the grass cover has not been damaged. Grass seeds are also sown after a while, and grass grows back in the places where drilling takes place." He said that now his father also works on a drilling rig. "I hope my children will study hard, learn technical skills and find stable jobs with reliable incomes in the future!" Tang told the Global Times that Yikebali's story illustrates how CNNC has embraced the concept of "green mining." The company maintains that the environmental impact of its mining operations is fully controllable. It also gives priority to hiring local villagers and their relatives, allowing residents to benefit directly from the projects. At the same time, the company's tax contributions support local government finances and help promote additional employment and economic development. Together, these efforts have helped win the acceptance of local communities. From the arduous drilling work carried out by generations of prospectors in the Gobi Desert and mountains to the application of third-generation neutral in-situ leaching technology on the Ili grasslands, the practices unfolding in this valley offer a vivid illustration of the high-quality development of China's nuclear industry. How has this path been forged? One detail that left a lasting impression on the Global Times reporter during the visit offers an answer. A slogan written on a wall inside the plant reads: "Responsibility, Safety, Innovation, Excellence." Perhaps these words hold the real key to CNNC's approach of "developing resources underground while protecting greenery above ground."

item.title: Mbappé's lesson: Talent opens doors, respect keeps them open
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 16:30:00
Kylian Mbappé Photo: VCG A football star can make hundreds of millions on the pitch, only to lose the trust of an entire market by failing to show the most basic respect. French football star Kylian Mbappé has recently sparked a fierce backlash in China after making extremely inappropriate remarks in a recent interview. What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it. Dongqiudi, a major Chinese football news and community platform, issued a statement saying that it would not translate the interview because the footballer's remarks had hurt the feelings of Chinese fans and the Chinese people. Brands including Dongpeng Beverage Group and Chinese dairy giant Mengniu promptly terminated their cooperation. This is not an emotional outburst, but a rational choice made spontaneously by the market. On Tuesday, Mbappé apologized. In a statement, he wrote "my comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world." The lesson is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn't get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance. Mbappé's talent and skills are beyond doubt. But talent and public responsibility are two entirely different things. The first determines how many goals you score and how much you are worth; the second determines how many people are still willing to pay for you. Talent may open the door to a market, but respect is what keeps it open. We don't know whether Mbappé would deliberately set out to offend a country whose market has helped fuel his commercial success. One thing is for sure: He lacks cross-cultural awareness, and fails to appreciate the responsibilities that come with global fame. Had he shown even a basic understanding of Chinese culture and sensitivities, he might have thought twice before speaking so disrespectfully. Every culture has its boundaries. That is no secret. No one expects a foreign athlete to be an expert on China. But global superstars who have long profited from commercial partnerships in China should make an effort to understand the country's cultural sensitivities and show a basic level of respect. That is not asking for special treatment. It is basic commercial common sense. For Chinese brands, terminating such cooperation is no small decision. Previous marketing investments, contractual obligations and the cost of replacing promotional materials all mean real costs. Yet, by cutting ties, these companies are sending a clear message: When public sentiment is offended, businesses cannot pretend nothing has happened. China's market remains open and welcomes athletes and brands from around the world to share in its opportunities. But an open market is not a market without boundaries. The threshold is respect. Those who disregard the feelings of the Chinese people should not expect to escape the commercial consequences. For decades, some international public figures have been happy to take the money from the Chinese market while talking carelessly about China. When it comes to matters of principle, they tend to dismiss offensive remarks as "personal expression" or hide behind "freedom of speech." That's no excuse. This time, Mbappé has learned the hard way. His case should serve as a clear red line for every foreign public figure hoping to profit from China: On issues of national sentiment, no one has the freedom to act recklessly. Going forward, our commercial contracts might as well spell out clearer clauses governing public conduct. The national feelings of the Chinese people are not to be provoked, and the Chinese market will leave no room for those who display arrogance and disrespect.

item.title: China's upgraded Jiaolong submersible completes 7,000-meter-class sea trials
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 16:11:00
China's upgraded manned deep-sea submersible Jiaolong is recovered on October 2, 2026, after completing its 465th dive, during which it reached a depth of 7,056.9 meters. Photo: Xinhua China's upgraded manned deep-sea submersible Jiaolong has successfully completed multiple 7,000-meter-class sea trials in the Philippine Basin, confirming the reliability and safety of the upgraded submersible and its domestically produced key components and strengthening China's technological edge in manned deep-sea exploration equipment, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Tuesday. The sea trials were conducted as part of the second leg of China's 100th oceanographic expedition. The submersible completed three test dives in the Philippine Basin, including two dives to depths exceeding 7,000 meters, reaching a maximum depth of 7,056.9 meters. All test parameters met the requirements for 7,000-meter-class sea trials. Sun Yongfu, a researcher at the National Deep Sea Center, said the sea trials fully verified the reliability and safety of Jiaolong following its iterative upgrades and the replacement of key components with domestically produced alternatives, consolidating and enhancing China's technological advantages in manned deep-sea submersible technology. Before the scientific expedition, the submersible received major upgrades, including a 7,000-meter-class high-energy-density lithium battery pack, domestically developed low-noise DC thrusters and advanced hydraulic and imaging systems. The upgrades introduced technological innovations across key components and systems, including power supply, propulsion, hydraulics, electrical systems, and communication and observation, significantly enhancing the submersible's operational capabilities. According to Sun, following its upgrades and the localization of key components, the submersible conducted multiple scientific missions in different sea areas to investigate deep-sea resources and marine ecosystems. These scientific expeditions will further deepen international cooperation in marine science, significantly advancing China's deep-sea exploration and research, and contribute to the country's goal of becoming a maritime power, Sun said. Global Times
